newsitem.title: ITALY: HPI, Marzotto link-up to create major textile firm.
newsitem.headline: HPI, Marzotto link-up to create major textile firm.

text.p: Italian industrial company HPI, newly formed in a spin-off from financial holding Gemina, announced at the weekend it planned to merge with textiles and clothing company Marzotto.
Holding di Partecipazioni Industriali (HPI) and Marzotto, owner of the German menswear label Hugo Boss, said in a statement the new company would be called Gruppo Industriale Marzotto.
"The proposed operation will create one of the largest groups worldwide in the textiles and clothing sector with a significant position in the editorial (publishing) sector," HPI and Marzotto said.
HPI's spin-off from Gemina has meant the transfer to HPI of textile groups Fila and GFT, as well as editorial unit RCS Editori.
Marzotto and HPI said they saw great potential for synergy between operations in the clothing and textiles sectors.

Based on preliminary results for 1996 from the two groups, the new company would have had an estimated turnover of 8.24 trillion lire ($4.85 billion) last year, a net profit of around 253 billion and staff totalling more than 21,000, they said.

HPI has just formally completed its separation from Gemina, the financial holding which 18 months ago was part of a failed merger dubbed SuperGemina and involving agri-industrial group Montedison, financial holding Ferruzzi (now Compart) and some Fiat car group companies.
HPI is due to be quoted on the Milan stock market from Monday. It now controls the industrial interests formerly owned by Gemina.
The incorporation must be approved by antitrust authorities and both companies' boards in meetings set for March 26.
The new group will be chaired by Pietro Marzotto, current chairman of the Marzotto family company, who is to replace HPI chairman Nicolo Nefri when the merger is complete.
The proposed managing director is HPI board member Maurizio Romiti, son of Cesare Romiti, the head of Fiat.

The groups have already worked out a proposed share swap ratio, with 13 ordinary HPI shares with a nominal value of 500 lire for one ordinary Marzotto share with a nominal value of 1,000 lire, and eight non-convertible HPI savings shares for one non-convertible Marzotto savings share.

Marzotto shares closed down 190 lire at 13,450 on the Milan stock market on Friday, shortly before it announced a consolidated net profit for 1996 of 58.1 billion lire, up from 50.1 billion in 1995, and a turnover of 2.225 trillion lire.

Marzotto and HPI said the new company would have a portfolio of significant stakes in various Italian companies, including 20.9 percent in paper group Cartiere Burgo, 25 percent of household furnishings company Zucchi and one percent or less stakes in banks Credito Italiano, Banca Commerciale Italiana and Mediobanca.
In addition it would have "cash resources at the parent level of the order of 1.0 trillion lire which will permit it to deal with investments necessary to reinforce its activities."

Providing shareholders exercised all their warrants, the biggest single shareholder in the eventual Gruppo Industriale Marzotto was estimated to be Fiat with a 17.3 percent stake, followed by the Marzotto family with 12.4 percent.
Investment bank Mediobanca was expected to hold 10 percent. A new shareholder syndicate would regroup around 40 percent of the company's capital.
"No syndicate member would have a stake which would give it a determining influence within the pact.

"Fiat and Mediobanca have also signalled the intention to make parts of their stakes available to let in new members ready to contribute in a stable fashion to the development of the new company and who would also participate in the pact," they said.
